title: #22 Ask students to respond in full sentences
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Craig Barton examines a common Cold Call exchange in maths classrooms, teacher asks a question, waits, calls a named student, waits again before evaluating, and argues it can be improved by requiring students to respond in full sentences rather than fragments. He gives three reasons: fragmented answers separated from the question stem are close to meaningless out of context, whereas a full-sentence response reconnects them into something worth remembering; full-sentence speech may help develop full-sentence writing, which he ties to a conversation with literacy expert Alex Quigley about the gap between spoken and written registers and to GCSE examiners' reports on students struggling with extended-response questions; and full-sentence answers give students who briefly lost focus a better chance to reconstruct meaning, since the question and answer are stated together rather than scattered across the exchange. He closes by noting students may resist the request and that teachers should explain the rationale rather than simply imposing it.
points: Sentence fragments like "base multiplied by perpendicular height, divided by two," spoken apart from the question, are close to meaningless on their own; folding the question into the answer makes the response memorable as a unit.
Requiring full-sentence responses may transfer to full-sentence writing, addressing a gap Barton has seen in GCSE examiners' reports where students struggle with explain/describe/discuss questions.
Students who briefly lost attention have a better chance of following along when the answer restates the question, rather than relying on a fragment spoken seconds after the prompt.
Because students may resist an unfamiliar request, Barton recommends explicitly explaining the rationale for full-sentence responses rather than just mandating it.
quotes: There is another improvement that could be made, and it is one I rarely see in maths classrooms: the requirement for students to respond in complete sentences.
In the first version of the exchange, the first and second parts of the statement are separated, both by time and additional dialogue.
But when combined with the first part of the statement, we have something that makes sense and is worth remembering.

The way we speak is often very different to the way we write, so if we can promote this more formal way of responding, it could provide a smoother transition for when we ask students to write in full sentences.
A cursory look through any maths GCSE examiner’s report reveals just how much students struggle with questions that ask them to explain, describe and discuss.
In the second version of the exchange, with the question and answer united, Isaac has a better chance of making sense of it.
As with many teaching strategies, it is a good idea to explain to students why you want them to do this.
